$doc: THE DISPATCH SURFACE — one declaration, two shells (#339).
Both shells marshal every post-boot .NET entry through a single serial lane.
Each method below declares whether it RETURNS IMMEDIATELY after queueing work
(fire-and-forget) or BLOCKS the caller until the work completes (blocking).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: dispatchHostEvent existed in both shells, spelled
identically, and blocked in one. The Swift body was written for the deep-link
caller, where Android uses dispatchHostEventAndWait; the LIFECYCLE caller was
later pointed at the same method. On a device the permission sheet raises a
lifecycle event while an async host call holds the lane, and the app dies.
No name generator could have caught it -- the names match perfectly and the
WHAT THE PIN CHECKS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: DispatchSurfaceDriftTests asserts
each shell declares the methods listed here and that each method's LANE CALL
matches its declared semantics. It reads SOURCE. It does not observe blocking
at runtime -- a genuinely behavioural cross-shell pin would need a JVM test and
an XCTest that agree with each other, which is itself an unpinned twin.
TO ADD A METHOD: add it here, implement it in both shells, and run the pin. If
it genuinely belongs to one shell only, give it a `platforms` list AND a
`reason` -- asymmetry is allowed, silence is not.

methods.name: dispatchEvent
methods.doc: A UI event from a control target. Non-zero rc routes to onError.

methods.name: dispatchEventAndWait
methods.reason: Consumed only by InspectorHost, a JVM-only developer tool with no iOS counterpart. Requiring a Swift twin would manufacture dead code to satisfy a guard.

methods.name: dispatchHostEvent
methods.doc: A host-initiated event. LIFECYCLE uses this. #339 is what happens when it blocks.

methods.name: dispatchHostEventAndWait
methods.doc: Deep-link and back: the caller needs the rc and needs frames applied before it returns.
